"Every morning, a sorrow comes forth from the wheel of time." Upon hearing the news of the imprisonment of my dear friend and brother Dr. Mostafa Mehraeen to serve an eight-year sentence, I was truly grieved; just as I am bitterly saddened for other political prisoners, and I pray from the bottom of my heart for the freedom of each and every one of them. Mehraeen, in the role of a knowledgeable and compassionate sociologist, has earnestly, courageously, and honestly expressed his frank and unvarnished criticisms of the ineffective style of governance in the country through his pen and his loud voice, like my dear Mostafa Tajzadeh. No matter how much I think, the issuance of harsh and severe sentences and the imprisonment of these elites carries no weight on the scales of justice and fairness, and is truly an oppressive act... For more than three decades, I have sat at the table of the wisdom and literature of Hafez Shirazi and have learned from him as much as I could. A few days ago, it was the twentieth of Mehr, coinciding with the commemoration day of this genius of Shiraz; the rogue of stoic thought who, in his elegant ghazals, in addition to addressing philosophical and existential matters, had a critical eye on the record of the ascetics, preachers, jurists, and Sufis of his time, and by observing what was happening around him, would cry out in pain: They count hypocrisy as lawful and the cup of wine as forbidden — what a path and creed, what a sharia and faith. And: They closed the door of the tavern, O God, do not allow that they open the door of the house of hypocrisy and pretense. And: Drink wine, for a hundred sins concealed by others are better than a devotion performed with pretense and hypocrisy. Sadly, we live in circumstances where the Minister of Education insists on "compulsory prayer," and after several years since the blessed movement "Woman, Life, Freedom," "unveiling" is criminalized; measures from which the smell of coercion and hypocrisy is clearly sensed. At the same time, in addition to insisting on carrying out executions whose cases, by the testimony of experts, lacked proper and defensible due process; intellectuals and political activists who radiate liberty, honesty, and courage from head to toe taste the flavor of imprisonment, torment, and prison. It is clear in such a sorrowful and dust-covered situation, on which pivot the wheel turns and to what extent governance has strayed from the orbit of fairness, justice, and effectiveness, and how much has been added to the volume of citizens' suffering... https://www.instagram.com/p/DecUHUpxz-N/?obrf=MXhmdzhrMjcyNWdiNA==

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] Excerpts from my recent interview with the IBNA book news agency: "If Sohrab…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

Excerpts from my recent interview with the IBNA book news agency: "If Sohrab were alive today, in the third millennium and in today's Tehran, and were present at his exhibitions, which part of what he had to say would be more worth hearing, and what would your first question to him be?" In my view, Sohrab's calmness, composure, and Stoic way of being would take on great significance; a subject about which much could be said separately. This calmness manifests in his lovemaking with and proximity to nature and a kind of "ataraxia," meaning inner tranquility, which the Stoic philosophers spoke about. Sohrab had internalized this calmness and also looked upon the world with a poetic gaze. The critique of technology, which I spoke about earlier, death-awareness and the effort to give meaning to life are also among the hearable and contemporary parts of his thought. Loving nature, paying attention to the other, and reflecting on categories such as death, love, solitude, and suffering can, in my view, still be worth hearing today. Regarding the exhibition of his paintings that you mentioned, naturally the paintings themselves matter; but I think Sohrab's words about the world and his way of living are also very important today. The reason is that in his case, there was considerable overlap between his public and private life, between his lived life and his work. He lived the way he wrote, and especially the way he composed poetry. This overlap and what we call "authenticity" can make a person charismatic and influence others; an unpretentious and intimate influence, such that one could benefit from his company and not feel the passage of time. In such conditions, the person's own presence and way of living become as important as his words. If I want to answer your question, "If you saw Sohrab, what would your first question to him be?" The truth is, I might not have had any specific question at all. For more than thirty years I have been living in Sohrab's atmosphere. Perhaps I would have liked to watch him; or, to put it better, to spend time in his company from noon until night, to chat together and experience that composure and calmness that was in his being, in socializing with him. I wanted to benefit, to the extent of my capacity, from that calmness that I believe had descended upon him. Sohrab himself said: "We ourselves are the awning of our calmness." I would have liked to catch and experience a breeze of that composure and calmness from his company... When you know someone well and are familiar with their life-world, sometimes sitting in silence itself, and even conversation without sound, can be valuable and instructive.👇👇👇 https://www.instagram.com/reel/DeR92wHRn21/?dlrf=dXF3aTRnY2t1ZTVs

entry.title: [Soroushdabbagh_Official] 13. Sohrab Sepehri was murmuring to himself somewhere in the "Traveler"…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @Soroushdabbagh_Official

13. Sohrab Sepehri was murmuring to himself somewhere in the "Traveler" notebook: "The journey carried me to equatorial lands / and beneath the shade of that tall green 'Banyan' / how well I remember / the phrase that entered the summer pasture of the mind: / Be vast, and alone, and humble, and hard." Sohrab, in his long-extended inner journey—which is of the nature of "horizontal wayfaring," setting out from oneself and arriving at oneself—draws back the curtain on his lived experience and pure illuminations; an experience that occurred beneath a towering tree, caught him unawares, drew him in, and like the Buddha enlightened him and granted him illumination. An experience that blew toward him and suffused every limb of his body and soul, marked a "rebirth" for him, and added to the volume of his "dove-like experiences"... Having breadth of spirit and a capacious digestive capacity makes you and me people of tolerance and civility, and noticeably increases our measure of "tolerance," "respecting the human being," and "accepting the other." Likewise, embracing "existential loneliness"—which is intertwined with your and my being—and reducing its volume with the aid of "velvety solitude," migrates lightness and joy toward us. "Humility and hardness" arrive together with high "self-esteem" and "self-worth" and are among the components of adequate mental health. "Humility" arrives with "realistic modesty," not "affected modesty." The modern wayfarer neither knows nor presents himself as lower than he is, nor considers and displays himself as higher than he is. He loves himself honestly and realistically, as he is, and with an eye to his endowments, capabilities, successes, weaknesses, misfortunes, and failures, deeply; and does not spend night and day seeking others' approval; rather, in Shamlou's phrase, he dwells at the "glorious altitude of humility" and fills and empties his lungs with its pure air. However, in "affected modesty," which is intertwined with low self-esteem, the individual does not believe in what he expresses about himself and in how he behaves, and with the affectation and artificiality that drips from his speech and behavior, he cunningly seeks to obtain others' approval. To the extent that you and I are "vast and alone and humble and hard," we are in a good state and experience mature dealings and relationships with the humans around us; for our existential goblet is filled, and following the Rendi of the Stoic-thinking Shirazi, we flow and drink and give drink.

Quoted from the book: Velvety Murmurs: Existential Whispers, Volume Two.
Author: Soroush Dabbagh
